laboureur.label: Laboureur (ploughman-farmer)
laboureur.summary: A comparatively well-off farmer who owned a plough team and worked his own land.
laboureur.text: A "laboureur" owned (or rented) a team of oxen or horses together with a plough, which made him one of the wealthier members of the Ancien Régime peasantry. He is distinct from the simple farmhand or day-labourer, who owned no plough team and hired out his labour instead. The term appears very frequently in French parish and civil registers from the 17th to the 19th century.

meunier.label: Meunier (miller)
meunier.summary: Operator of a mill, responsible for grinding the villagers' grain.
meunier.text: The miller operated a water or wind mill and turned the parish's grain into flour, keeping a portion as payment (the "mouture"). The trade was often hereditary, with the mill itself rented from the local lord or abbey.

tisserand.label: Tisserand (weaver)
tisserand.summary: Craftsman weaving linen or wool cloth on a hand loom.
tisserand.text: The weaver worked fibre (flax, hemp or wool) on a hand loom to produce cloth, frequently on commission for a merchant-clothier. Widespread in textile-producing regions (Normandy, Flanders, the Beauvaisis), the trade was often a supplementary activity alongside a small farm holding.

forgeron.label: Forgeron (blacksmith)
forgeron.summary: Craftsman working iron at the forge fire to make tools and fittings.
forgeron.text: The blacksmith heated and hammered iron to make or repair farm tools, cart fittings and horseshoes. A central village figure, he was sometimes also the farrier when he shod horses and oxen as well.

notaire.label: Notaire (notary)
notaire.summary: Public officer who drafted and kept legal deeds.
notaire.text: The notary was a royal (later republican) public officer responsible for drafting and preserving legal deeds: marriage contracts, probate inventories, property sales, wills. Notarial records are among the richest sources for genealogy, often far more detailed than parish registers.
